ref-033d040ec33958a8b08a.text:
The discovery modules used with Duqu can collect information on process details.
Modules can be pushed to and executed by Duqu that copy data to a staging area, compress it, and XOR encrypt it.
Duqu uses a custom command and control protocol that communicates over commonly used ports, and is frequently encapsulated by application layer protocols.
The reconnaissance modules used with Duqu can collect information on network configuration.
Adversaries can instruct Duqu to spread laterally by copying itself to shares it has enumerated and for which it has obtained legitimate credentials (via keylogging or other means). The remote host is then infected by using the compromised credentials to schedule a task on remote machines that executes the malware.
Duqu can track key presses with a keylogger module.
Duqu can be configured to have commands relayed over a peer-to-peer network of infected hosts if some of the hosts do not have Internet access.
Duqu creates a new service that loads a malicious driver when the system starts. When Duqu is active, the operating system believes that the driver is legitimate, as it has been signed with a valid private key.
Duqu will inject itself into different processes to evade detection. The selection of the target process is influenced by the security software that is installed on the system (Duqu will inject into different processes depending on which security suite is installed on the infected host).
Duqu is capable of loading executable code via process hollowing.
The discovery modules used with Duqu can collect information on open windows.
The Duqu command and control protocol's data stream can be encrypted with AES-CBC.
The discovery modules used with Duqu can collect information on network connections.
The discovery modules used with Duqu can collect information on accounts and permissions.
When the Duqu command and control is operating over HTTP or HTTPS, Duqu uploads data to its controller by appending it to a blank JPG file.
ref-033d040ec33958a8b08a.title: Symantec Security Response. (2011, November). W32.Duqu: The precursor to the next Stuxnet. Retrieved September 17, 2015.

ref-26932404df38b63eea54.text:
Pisloader has a command to upload a file to the victim machine.
Pisloader has a command to collect victim system information, including the system name and OS version.
Pisloader uses DNS as its C2 protocol.
Pisloader has a command to collect the victim's IP address.
Pisloader establishes persistence via a Registry Run key.
Pisloader uses cmd.exe to set the Registry Run key value. It also has a command to spawn a command shell.
Pisloader has commands to list drives on the victim machine and to list file information for a given directory.
Pisloader obfuscates files by splitting strings into smaller sub-strings and including "garbage" strings that are never used. The malware also uses return-oriented programming (ROP) technique and single-byte XOR to obfuscate data.
Responses from the Pisloader C2 server are base32-encoded.

ref-27769a411a26b4494c2c.text: OSX/Shlayer can escalate privileges to root by asking the user for credentials. OSX/Shlayer can masquerade as a Flash Player update. OSX/Shlayer can base64-decode and AES-decrypt downloaded payloads. Versions of OSX/Shlayer pass encrypted and password-protected code to openssl and then write the payload to the /tmp folder. If running with elevated privileges, OSX/Shlayer has used the spctl command to disable Gatekeeper protection for a downloaded file. OSX/Shlayer can also leverage system links pointing to bash scripts in the downloaded DMG file to bypass Gatekeeper, a flaw patched in macOS 11.3 and later versions. OSX/Shlayer has been Notarized by Apple, resulting in successful passing of additional Gatekeeper checks. OSX/Shlayer has executed a .command script from a hidden directory in a mounted DMG. OSX/Shlayer can use the chmod utility to set a file as executable, such as chmod 777 or chmod +x. OSX/Shlayer has relied on users mounting and executing a malicious DMG file. OSX/Shlayer has collected the IOPlatformUUID, session UID, and the OS version using the command sw_vers -productVersion. OSX/Shlayer can use bash scripts to check the macOS version, download payloads, and extract bytes from files. OSX/Shlayer uses the command sh -c tail -c +1381... to extract bytes at an offset from a specified file. OSX/Shlayer uses the curl -fsL "$url" >$tmp_path command to download malicious payloads into a temporary directory. OSX/Shlayer can download payloads, and extract bytes from files. OSX/Shlayer uses the curl -fsL "$url" >$tmp_path command to download malicious payloads into a temporary directory.
ref-27769a411a26b4494c2c.title: Carbon Black Threat Analysis Unit. (2019, February 12). New macOS Malware Variant of Shlayer (OSX) Discovered. Retrieved August 8, 2019.

ref-2eb276c76f3bd1f3ef0e.text:
SystemBC has collected the Windows account username on the victim machine.
SystemBC has used `cmd.exe` to execute VBS scripts, BAT scripts and CMD scripts.
SystemBC has used hidden scheduled tasks to execute PowerShell commands by adding the following: `-WindowStyle Hidden -ep bypass -file `.
SystemBC has encrypted its C2 traffic with RC4.
SystemBC has used multiple proxy layers, such as SOCKS5 and Tor, for C2 communication. SystemBC has also leveraged Tor for encrypting and concealing C2 traffic. The server component of SystemBC has used SOCKS5 for C2 communication.
SystemBC has downloaded additional files for execution on the victim’s machine. The server component of SystemBC has the ability to send additional files to victim machines.
SystemBC has utilized native Windows API functions such as `EnumWindows`and `GetVolumeInformationA` during discovery activities.
SystemBC has leveraged the Sleep functions before and after commands to ensure execution using the hexadecimal values within commands to include `Sleep(0x2710u)` that waits 10 seconds, and `Sleep(0xEA60u)` for 60 seconds.
SystemBC has executed a copy of itself as a scheduled task with the `start` command. The copy of SystemBC has random file and directory names within the ProgramData directory.
SystemBC has checked if the last characters of DNS server names end in .bit before initializing C2 communication. SystemBC has identified running processes associated with anti-virus solutions to include `a2guard.exe` to determine whether it executes or not.
SystemBC has leveraged VBScript to execute malicious code.
SystemBC has utilized the `-WindowStyle Hidden -ep bypass -file `to conceal PowerShell windows.
SystemBC has the ability to enumerate running processes.
ref-2eb276c76f3bd1f3ef0e.title: Gallagher, S., Gn, S. (2020, December 16). Ransomware operators use SystemBC RAT as off-the-shelf Tor backdoor. Retrieved May 16, 2025.

ref-45e68e56feb0a4d6fd15.text: Octopus can collect system drive and disk size information. Octopus has used HTTP GET and POST requests for C2 communications. Octopus can capture screenshots of the victims’ machine. Octopus has used wmic.exe for local discovery information. Octopus can collect the computer name, OS version, and OS architecture information. Octopus can collect information on the Windows directory and searches for compressed RAR files on the host. Octopus can collect the username from the victim’s machine. Octopus has uploaded stolen files and data from a victim's machine over its C2 channel. Octopus can download additional files and tools onto the victim’s machine. Octopus has stored collected information in the Application Data directory on a compromised host. Octopus has been disguised as legitimate programs, such as Java and Telegram Messenger. Octopus can collect the host IP address from the victim’s machine. Octopus has encoded C2 communications in Base64. Octopus achieved persistence by placing a malicious executable in the startup directory and has added the HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run key to the Registry.
ref-45e68e56feb0a4d6fd15.title: Kaspersky Lab's Global Research & Analysis Team. (2018, October 15). Octopus-infested seas of Central Asia. Retrieved November 14, 2018.

ref-589c605e1fd4470ec80a.text: Comnie executes the netstat -ano command. Comnie appends a total of 64MB of garbage data to a file to deter any security products in place that may be scanning files on disk. Comnie collects the hostname of the victim machine. Comnie attempts to detect several anti-virus products. Comnie uses HTTP for C2 communication. Comnie establishes persistence via a .lnk file in the victim’s startup path. Comnie uses RC4 and Base64 to obfuscate strings. Comnie encrypts command and control communications with RC4. Comnie runs the command: net start >> %TEMP%\info.dat on a victim. Comnie executes BAT scripts. Comnie executes a batch script to store discovery information in %TEMP%\info.dat and then uploads the temporarily file to the remote C2 server. Comnie uses the net user command. Comnie achieves persistence by adding a shortcut of itself to the startup path in the Registry. Comnie uses the tasklist to view running processes on the victim’s machine. Comnie executes VBS scripts. Comnie uses Rundll32 to load a malicious DLL. Comnie uses ipconfig /all and route PRINT to identify network adapter and interface information. Comnie uses blogs and third-party sites (GitHub, tumbler, and BlogSpot) to avoid DNS-based blocking of their communication to the command and control server.
ref-589c605e1fd4470ec80a.title: Grunzweig, J. (2018, January 31). Comnie Continues to Target Organizations in East Asia. Retrieved June 7, 2018.

ref-5e874bf3ddef27a8e97c.text: NavRAT leverages cmd.exe to perform discovery techniques. NavRAT loads malicious shellcode and executes it in memory. NavRAT uses tasklist /v to check running processes. NavRAT writes multiple outputs to a TMP file using the >> method. NavRAT uses systeminfo on a victim’s machine. NavRAT can download files remotely. NavRAT creates a Registry key to ensure a file gets executed upon reboot in order to establish persistence. NavRAT uses the email platform, Naver, for C2 communications, leveraging SMTP. NavRAT logs the keystrokes on the targeted system. NavRAT copies itself into a running Internet Explorer process to evade detection.
ref-5e874bf3ddef27a8e97c.title: Mercer, W., Rascagneres, P. (2018, May 31). NavRAT Uses US-North Korea Summit As Decoy For Attacks In South Korea. Retrieved June 11, 2018.

ref-624de41e7fa70a8cc616.text: TAINTEDSCRIBE can copy itself into the current user’s Startup folder as “Narrator.exe” for persistence. TAINTEDSCRIBE can download additional modules from its C2 server. TAINTEDSCRIBE can use DriveList to retrieve drive information. TAINTEDSCRIBE has used FakeTLS for session authentication. TAINTEDSCRIBE can randomly pick one of five hard-coded IP addresses for C2 communication; if one of the IP fails, it will wait 60 seconds and then try another IP address. TAINTEDSCRIBE can execute FileRecvWriteRand to append random bytes to the end of a file received from C2. TAINTEDSCRIBE uses a Linear Feedback Shift Register (LFSR) algorithm for network encryption. The TAINTEDSCRIBE main executable has disguised itself as Microsoft’s Narrator. TAINTEDSCRIBE can execute ProcessList for process discovery. TAINTEDSCRIBE can execute GetLocalTime for time discovery. TAINTEDSCRIBE can delete files from a compromised host. TAINTEDSCRIBE has used FileReadZipSend to compress a file and send to C2. TAINTEDSCRIBE can enable Windows CLI access and execute files. The TAINTEDSCRIBE command and execution module can perform target system enumeration. TAINTEDSCRIBE can change the timestamp of specified filenames. TAINTEDSCRIBE can use DirectoryList to enumerate files in a specified directory.
ref-624de41e7fa70a8cc616.title: USG. (2020, May 12). MAR-10288834-2.v1 – North Korean Trojan: TAINTEDSCRIBE. Retrieved March 5, 2021.

ref-76847ae693931dda509f.text:
TrickBot module shareDll/mshareDll discovers network shares via the WNetOpenEnumA API.
TrickBot uses brute-force attack against RDP with rdpscanDll module.
TrickBot uses vncDll module to remote control the victim machine.
TrickBot uses module networkDll for process list discovery.
ref-76847ae693931dda509f.title: Tudorica, R., Maximciuc, A., Vatamanu, C. (2020, March 18). New TrickBot Module Bruteforces RDP Connections, Targets Select Telecommunication Services in US and Hong Kong. Retrieved March 15, 2021.

ref-b6c797d8276519559354.text:
Pcexter has the ability to search for files in specified directories.
The Ninja loader can call Windows APIs for discovery, process injection, and payload decryption.
Ninja can enumerate processes on a targeted host.
Pcexter can upload stolen files to OneDrive storage accounts via HTTP `POST`.
Ninja can obtain the computer name and information on the OS from targeted hosts.
Ninja has compressed its data with the LZSS algorithm.
LoFiSe can collect all the files from the working directory every three hours and place them into a password-protected archive for further exfiltration.
Ninja can forward TCP packets between the C2 and a remote host.
LoFiSe can save files to be evaluated for further exfiltration in the `C:\Programdata\Microsoft\` and `C:\windows\temp\` folders.
Pcexter can upload files from targeted systems.
The Ninja loader component can decrypt and decompress the payload.
Ninja can proxy C2 communications including to and from internal agents without internet connectivity.
Ninja has used legitimate looking filenames for its loader including update.dll and x64.dll.
The Ninja payload is XOR encrypted and compressed. Ninja has also XORed its configuration data with a constant value of `0xAA`.
Ninja loader components can be executed through rundll32.exe.
LoFiSe can collect files of interest from targeted systems.
Ninja loaders can be side-loaded with legitimate and signed executables including the VLC.exe media player.
LoFiSe can monitor the file system to identify files less than 6.4 MB in size with file extensions including .doc, .docx, .xls, .xlsx, .ppt, .pptx, .pdf, .rtf, .tif, .odt, .ods, .odp, .eml, and .msg.
LoFiSe can collect files into password-protected ZIP-archives for exfiltration.
Ninja has the ability to enumerate directory content.
Pcexter has been distributed and executed as a DLL file named Vspmsg.dll via DLL side-loading.
Ninja can obtain information on physical drives from targeted hosts.
LoFiSe has been executed as a file named DsNcDiag.dll through side-loading.
Ninja has the ability to inject an agent module into a new process and arbitrary shellcode into running processes.
ref-b6c797d8276519559354.title: Dedola, G. et al. (2023, October 12). ToddyCat: Keep calm and check logs. Retrieved January 3, 2024.

ref-bfb8998261b241268a7a.text:
Emotet inflates malicious files and malware as an evasion technique.
Emotet uses obfuscated URLs to download a ZIP file.
Emotet uses RegSvr32 to execute the DLL payload.
Emotet uses a copy of `certutil.exe` stored in a temporary directory for process hollowing, starting the program in a suspended state before loading malicious code.
ref-bfb8998261b241268a7a.title: Kenefick, I. (2023, March 13). Emotet Returns, Now Adopts Binary Padding for Evasion. Retrieved June 19, 2024.

ref-d5fdeba5ee51cbe00a7b.text:
MoonWind can obtain the victim hostname, Windows version, RAM amount, and screen resolution.
MoonWind encrypts C2 traffic using RC4 with a static key.
MoonWind has a command to return a list of running processes.
MoonWind saves information from its keylogging routine as a .zip file in the present working directory.
MoonWind communicates over ports 80, 443, 53, and 8080 via raw sockets instead of the protocols usually associated with the ports.
MoonWind installs itself as a new service with automatic startup to establish persistence. The service checks every 60 seconds to determine if the malware is running; if not, it will spawn a new instance.
MoonWind can execute commands via an interactive command shell. MoonWind uses batch scripts for various purposes, including to restart and uninstall itself.
MoonWind completes network communication via raw sockets.
MoonWind has a command to return a directory listing for a specified directory.
MoonWind has a keylogger.
MoonWind obtains the number of removable drives from the victim.
MoonWind can obtain the number of drives on the victim machine.
MoonWind obtains the victim's current time.
MoonWind obtains the victim IP address.
MoonWind can delete itself or specified files.
MoonWind obtains the victim username.
ref-d5fdeba5ee51cbe00a7b.title: Miller-Osborn, J. and Grunzweig, J.. (2017, March 30). Trochilus and New MoonWind RATs Used In Attack Against Thai Organizations. Retrieved March 30, 2017.

ref-e3e5ca0b33cfeab93876.text:
Manjusaka data exfiltration takes place over HTTP channels.
Manjusaka can gather information about specific files on the victim system.
Manjusaka performs basic system profiling actions to fingerprint and register the victim system with the C2 controller.
Manjusaka extracts credentials from the Windows Registry associated with Premiumsoft Navicat, a utility used to facilitate access to various database types.
Manjusaka has used HTTP for command and control communication.
Manjusaka gathers credentials from Chromium-based browsers.
Manjusaka gathers information about current network connections, local and remote addresses associated with them, and associated processes.
Manjusaka communication includes a client-created session cookie with base64-encoded information representing information from the victim system.
Manjusaka can execute arbitrary commands passed to it from the C2 controller via `cmd.exe /c`.
Manjusaka can take screenshots of the victim desktop.
ref-e3e5ca0b33cfeab93876.title: Asheer Malhotra & Vitor Ventura. (2022, August 2). Manjusaka: A Chinese sibling of Sliver and Cobalt Strike. Retrieved September 4, 2024.

ref-f2dd3e5584596d6ea27a.text: Gold Dragon collects endpoint information using the systeminfo command. RunningRAT captures keystrokes and sends them back to the C2 server. RunningRAT contains code to compress files. Gold Dragon collects the endpoint victim's username and uses it as a basis for downloading additional components from the C2 server. Brave Prince gathers file and directory information from the victim’s machine. Gold Dragon stores information gathered from the endpoint in a file named 1.hwp. Gold Dragon can download additional components from the C2 server. Some Brave Prince variants have used South Korea's Daum email service to exfiltrate information, and later variants have posted the data to a web server via an HTTP post command. Brave Prince lists the running processes. RunningRAT kills antimalware running process. Gold Dragon encrypts data using Base64 before being sent to the command and control server. Gold Dragon checks for anti-malware products and processes. RunningRAT contains code to delete files from the victim’s machine. Gold Dragon establishes persistence in the Startup folder. Brave Prince terminates antimalware processes. RunningRAT contains code to open and copy data from the clipboard. Gold Dragon uses cmd.exe to execute commands for discovery. RunningRAT contains code to clear event logs. RunningRAT gathers logical drives information and volume information. Gold Dragon enumerates registry keys with the command regkeyenum and obtains information for the Registry key HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Gold Dragon terminates anti-malware processes if they’re found running on the system. RunningRAT uses a batch file to kill a security program task and then attempts to remove itself. Brave Prince collects hard drive content and system configuration information. RunningRAT gathers the OS version and processor information. Gold Dragon uses HTTP for communication to the control servers. Gold Dragon lists the directories for Desktop, program files, and the user’s recently accessed files. Brave Prince gathers network configuration information as well as the ARP cache. RunningRAT adds itself to the Registry key Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run to establish persistence upon reboot. Gold Dragon checks the running processes on the victim’s machine. Brave Prince gathers information about the Registry. Gold Dragon deletes one of its files, 2.hwp, from the endpoint after establishing persistence.
ref-f2dd3e5584596d6ea27a.title: Sherstobitoff, R., Saavedra-Morales, J. (2018, February 02). Gold Dragon Widens Olympics Malware Attacks, Gains Permanent Presence on Victims’ Systems. Retrieved June 6, 2018.

ref-fc116a6180ca8d3d8b40.text: MacSpy uses Tor for command and control. Proton persists via Launch Agent. FruitFly has the ability to list processes on the system. FruitFly executes and stores obfuscated Perl scripts. FruitFly saves itself with a leading "." to make it a hidden file. Proton prompts users for their credentials. MacSpy uses HTTP for command and control. iKitten saves itself with a leading "." so that it's hidden from users by default. Proton uses VNC to connect into systems. FruitFly persists via a Launch Agent. Proton removes logs from /var/logs and /Library/logs. FruitFly takes screenshots of the user's desktop. MacSpy persists via a Launch Agent. Proton gathers credentials in files for keychains. Proton gathers credentials for Google Chrome. FruitFly will delete files on the system. Proton uses macOS' .command file type to script actions. iKitten will zip up the /Library/Keychains directory before exfiltrating it. MacSpy can capture screenshots of the desktop over multiple monitors. Dok prompts the user for credentials. Proton captures the content of the desktop with the screencapture binary. MacSpy captures keystrokes. FruitFly looks for specific files and file types. Proton uses an encrypted file to store commands and configuration values. iKitten lists the current processes running. iKitten adds an entry to the rc.common file for persistence. iKitten collects the keychains on the system. Proton zips up files before exfiltrating them. Proton uses a keylogger to capture keystrokes. Proton removes all files in the /tmp directory. Proton kills security tools like Wireshark that are running. Dok installs a root certificate to aid in Adversary-in-the-Middle actions using the command add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain /tmp/filename. Proton modifies the tty_tickets line in the sudoers file. iKitten will look for the current IP address. MacSpy can steal clipboard contents. Dok uses AppleScript to create a login item for persistence. iKitten prompts the user for their credentials. MacSpy can record the sounds from microphones on a computer. Proton gathers credentials in files for 1password. Dok downloads and installs Tor via homebrew.
ref-fc116a6180ca8d3d8b40.title: Patrick Wardle. (n.d.). Mac Malware of 2017. Retrieved September 21, 2018.
